evaluated.name: LossGatedGrossProfitCoverage
evaluated.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(NEG(pi), 0), IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), lt)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Among firms currently reporting a pretax loss (the distress state), the ones whose gross profit still covers a large fraction of total liabilities have a viable operating core and recover, while loss-makers whose gross profit is small relative to obligations face restructuring; for profitable firms this coverage difference carries little default information.
evaluated.reasoning: The pretax-loss indicator switches the signal on only in the distressed state and leaves healthy firms at the neutral value zero, so the predictive content is genuinely state-dependent rather than an unconditional gross-profitability effect. Gross profit (revt minus cogs) is the most persistent quality flow available and is unpolluted by the write-offs and one-off charges that drive reported losses.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: MarginDecayXCashDrain
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(TREND(RATIO(cogs, revt), 5)), IND_RANK(NEG(DELTA(RATIO(che, at), 1))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Distress is a process, not a level: firms whose cost-of-sales ratio has been trending up for years (eroding gross margin quality) and which are simultaneously drawing down their cash buffer are on a depletion path that the market prices with a lag, producing low subsequent returns.
evaluated.reasoning: Neither a slow margin slide nor a single year of cash decline is alarming alone; jointly they indicate that internal funds are shrinking exactly as unit economics deteriorate. Using a 5-year trend for the quality channel and a one-year change for the liquidity channel matches the different speeds at which operating deterioration and financing stress manifest.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: MarginStabilityXPretaxDebtCoverage
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(pi, lt)), IND_RANK(NEG(VOL(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), revt), 5))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Pretax earnings coverage of total liabilities is a much more reliable solvency measure when the underlying gross margin is stable; firms with strong coverage and stable margins are safe and richly rewarded, while weak coverage combined with volatile margins marks unpriced default risk.
evaluated.reasoning: Gross-margin volatility is the quality dimension that determines how much information a single year's coverage ratio contains, so multiplying the two ranks sharpens the distress ordering instead of restating it. Pretax income (pi) is used rather than net income to avoid tax and special-item noise in the coverage channel.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: NegativeWorkingCapitalProfitSort
evaluated.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(NEG(wcap), 0), IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Negative working capital is ambiguous: for profitable firms it reflects efficient supplier financing and fast inventory turns, but for weakly profitable firms it is a liquidity shortfall. Sorting the negative-working-capital subsample on gross profitability should therefore generate a large spread, with efficient operators outperforming genuinely illiquid firms.
evaluated.reasoning: This tests a sign-interpretation flip rather than a monotone composite: the same balance-sheet configuration means opposite things depending on operating quality, which no single-theme signal can express. Firms with positive working capital are held at neutral zero so the spread is driven entirely by the conditioned subsample.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: CapitalConsumptionAdjustedLiquidity
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(oancf, dp), at)), IND_RANK(RATIO(che, lt)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Operating cash flow flatters firms whose cash flow is mostly the depreciation add-back; subtracting dp isolates cash earnings net of capital consumption, and this true cash-generating capacity is what makes a given cash-to-liabilities buffer sustainable rather than a one-time stock.
evaluated.reasoning: The interaction separates firms whose liquidity is replenished by real economic earnings from those holding a static cash stock while consuming their asset base, a distinction invisible to either cash-flow or liquidity signals alone. Depreciation intensity also proxies for the reinvestment obligation that competes with debt service.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: ChronicLossShortRunway
evaluated.expression: MUL(TS_SUM(INDICATOR(NEG(pi), 0), 5), IND_ZSCORE(NEG(RATIO(che, cogs))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Repeated pretax losses only become terminal when the cash balance is small relative to the firm's operating cost base; the number of loss years over five years times the shortness of the cash runway (che scaled by cogs) identifies firms most likely to dilute or default, which underperform.
evaluated.reasoning: Cash divided by cost of goods sold is an explicit runway concept that fuses the liquidity stock with the operating burn rate, and multiplying it by loss persistence rather than a single-year loss flag removes transitory-loss firms from the short leg. Firms with no loss years receive zero and stay neutral, so the spread comes from the chronically unprofitable tail.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: LiquidCoverageOfCurrentObligations
evaluated.expression: RATIO(ADD(che, SUB(oancf, dp)), lct)
evaluated.hypothesis: Near-term default risk is governed by the sum of the liquid stock (cash) and the sustainable cash flow net of capital consumption, measured against the obligations actually coming due (current liabilities); firms with high combined coverage earn higher returns than firms whose current liabilities exceed both their cash and their true cash earnings.
evaluated.reasoning: This fuses the quality flow (oancf net of the dp add-back) and the distress stock into a single economically interpretable coverage ratio rather than a product of ranks, which should raise coverage and stability relative to the gen-1 winner while preserving the mechanism. Current liabilities are strictly positive, so the ratio is well behaved and does not need the two-way ranking machinery.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: NetLiquidPositionXCashEarnings
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(oancf, dp), lt)), IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(che, dlc), at)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Refinancing risk, not total leverage, is the binding distress channel: firms whose cash exceeds short-term debt are immune to rollover shocks, and this immunity is most valuable when accompanied by cash earnings that actually service total liabilities. The joint group earns higher returns; net-short-cash firms with weak cash earnings underperform.
evaluated.reasoning: Replacing the cash-to-total-liabilities stock with the *net* liquid position (che minus dlc) changes the economic content from a liquidity buffer to rollover capacity, a distinct distress mechanism from the gen-1 winner. Scaling cash earnings by total liabilities rather than assets keeps both legs on a solvency footing.

evaluated.name: LossGatedCashRunway
evaluated.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(NEG(pi), 0), IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(che, cogs)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Among firms reporting a pretax loss, survival and returns are determined by how many periods of operating costs the cash balance can fund, not by the level of gross profitability; loss-makers with long runways are mispriced as if they were doomed and subsequently outperform loss-makers facing imminent financing needs.
evaluated.reasoning: This directly repairs the gen-1 loss-gate failure by keeping the state gate that isolated the distressed subsample but replacing the sorting variable with the liquidity-versus-burn concept that ChronicLossShortRunway's negative alpha already supported. Cash scaled by cost of goods sold is a runway measure that combines the distress stock with the operating cost base.

evaluated.name: ThinMarginCushionNoCash
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(cogs, revt)), IND_RANK(NEG(RATIO(che, lt))))
evaluated.hypothesis: A high cost-of-sales ratio means there is little gross-margin cushion to absorb a demand or input-price shock; when such a firm also holds almost no cash against its liabilities it has neither an operating nor a financial buffer, and its equity earns low subsequent returns.
evaluated.reasoning: This replaces the failed dynamic margin-decay design with the static level of the margin cushion, on the diagnosis that five-year trends and one-year cash changes were too noisy to identify the fragile group. The interaction is genuine: thin margins are tolerable with a cash buffer, and low cash is tolerable with fat margins, so only the joint state should predict underperformance.

evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(MA(RATIO(SUB(oancf, dp), at), 3)), IND_RANK(RATIO(che, lt)))
evaluated.hypothesis: The quality leg of the cash-earnings/liquidity interaction should reflect durable earning power rather than a single year's cash flow; three-year averaged cash earnings net of capital consumption, combined with the cash buffer against liabilities, should sharpen the distress ordering and improve the spread's reliability.

evaluated.name: WeakestLinkSolvency
evaluated.expression: MIN(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(oancf, dp), lt)), IND_RANK(RATIO(che, lct)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Solvency is a weakest-link property: a firm is safe only if both its cash-earnings coverage of total liabilities and its cash coverage of near-term obligations are adequate, and strength in one dimension does not substitute for weakness in the other. The minimum of the two ranks should therefore predict returns better than their product.
evaluated.reasoning: The product form rewards firms that are extreme on one leg, whereas default is triggered by the binding constraint, so the MIN operator matches the economics of financial distress more literally. Testing it against the multiplicative winner isolates the functional form while holding the two economic channels fixed.

evaluated.name: GrossProfitRolloverWeakestLink
evaluated.expression: MIN(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), lt)), IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(che, dlc), at)))
evaluated.hypothesis: The weakest-link solvency mechanism should not depend on the cash-flow statement: gross profit relative to total liabilities measures the same durable capacity to service obligations, and a firm is safe only if that capacity and its net liquid position (cash minus short-term debt) are both adequate.
evaluated.reasoning: This tests whether the archive's best mechanism is about economic solvency or about the specific oancf-minus-dp construction, while nearly doubling coverage because gross profit is available for firms and periods where cash-flow items are missing. If the alpha survives at higher coverage, the mechanism is robust rather than a sample artefact.

evaluated.name: CashEarningsRolloverWeakestLink
evaluated.expression: MIN(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(oancf, dp), lt)), IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(che, dlc), at)))

evaluated.name: TripleConstraintSolvency
evaluated.expression: MIN(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(oancf, dp), lt)), MIN(IND_RANK(RATIO(che, lct)), IND_RANK(RATIO(re, at))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Financial distress has three distinct binding constraints: insufficient cash earnings to service liabilities, insufficient cash for near-term obligations, and an absence of accumulated retained earnings (no equity cushion built from past profitability). A firm must clear all three to be genuinely safe, and the minimum across them should predict returns more sharply than any pair.
evaluated.reasoning: Retained earnings scaled by assets adds a stock-of-past-quality channel that neither the cash-flow nor the liquidity leg captures, and it is the classic Altman/Ohlson survival variable. Nesting MIN keeps the weakest-link economics that outperformed the multiplicative form.

evaluated.name: LiquidityDeteriorationUnderWeakCoverage
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(NEG(DELTA(RATIO(SUB(che, dlc), at), 1))), IND_RANK(NEG(RATIO(SUB(oancf, dp), lct))))

evaluated.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(NEG(SUB(che, dlc)), 0), IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(oancf, dp), lct)))

Safe firms are held at neutral zero so the spread is generated entirely inside the exposed subsample.

evaluated.name: BurnAdjustedTotalRunway
evaluated.expression: IND_RANK(RATIO(ADD(che, SUB(oancf, dp)), cogs))
evaluated.hypothesis: The economically correct distress metric is time, not a ratio to obligations: cash on hand plus this year's cash earnings net of capital consumption, expressed in units of the annual operating cost base, measures how long the firm can operate without external funding. Longer total runway predicts higher returns.

Scaling by cogs rather than by liabilities changes the economic content from a solvency ratio to a survival horizon, which is the distinct design choice being tested.

evaluated.hypothesis: A firm is genuinely safe only if its accrual operating margin, its cash earnings net of capital consumption, and its net liquid position are all adequate relative to obligations; requiring all three constraints to clear should isolate a cleaner safe/fragile ordering than any two of them.

If both alpha and Sharpe hold at higher coverage it becomes the preferred consolidation target.

evaluated.name: RolloverLegScaledByObligations
evaluated.expression: MIN(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(oancf, dp), lt)), IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(che, dlc), lt)))
evaluated.hypothesis: The net liquid position is economically meaningful relative to the obligations it must eventually meet rather than relative to the asset base; scaling both legs by total liabilities puts the solvency flow and the liquidity stock on a common denominator and should sharpen the ordering.
evaluated.reasoning: This isolates a single design choice - the denominator of the liquidity leg - holding the quality leg and the MIN aggregation fixed, so the result cleanly attributes performance to scaling rather than to economic content. Asset scaling mixes in capital intensity, which is a size/industry effect rather than a distress effect.

evaluated.name: AccrualGapUnderRolloverStress
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(pi, oancf), revt)), IND_RANK(NEG(RATIO(SUB(che, dlc), at))))

evaluated.reasoning: The accrual channel is untested in this archive and is economically distinct from the level-of-coverage channel: it measures the credibility of earnings rather than their size, and its relevance is conditional on financing slack. Scaling the gap by revenue keeps it comparable across capital structures while the second leg supplies the distress conditioning.

evaluated.expression: MIN(IND_RANK(TS_MIN(RATIO(SUB(oancf, dp), lt), 5)), IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(che, dlc), at)))

evaluated.reasoning: Smoothing with a three-year mean did not improve the multiplicative form, but a trough is a downside-risk concept rather than a noise-reduction device and speaks directly to default probability. If the Sharpe ratio rises while alpha holds, persistence of coverage - not its current level - is the priced characteristic.

evaluated.hypothesis: For firms with fat gross margins, carrying net debt is a compensated risk and a discipline device rather than a default threat, so within this high-quality group the most net-indebted firms should earn higher returns - the opposite of the unconditional distress effect.

Low-margin firms are held at neutral zero so the spread comes entirely from the conditioned high-quality group.

evaluated.hypothesis: A safe firm must clear three separate constraints: its worst-case cash earnings covered its liabilities, it holds cash in excess of short-term debt, and its reported income is backed by cash rather than accruals. considered.name: LeverageXEarningsInstability
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(lt, at)), IND_RANK(VOL(RATIO(ib, at), 5)))
considered.hypothesis: Balance-sheet leverage is only genuinely distressing when the earnings stream servicing it is unstable; firms that are simultaneously highly levered and have volatile ROA are the true financially fragile group whose equity earns low subsequent returns (the distress anomaly), whereas levered firms with stable earnings are merely leveraged, not distressed.
considered.reasoning: Leverage alone is a weak return predictor because stable cash generators can safely carry debt, so the distress effect must be sharpened by earnings-stability quality. Multiplying within-industry ranks of liabilities/assets and 5-year ROA volatility isolates the joint tail, where mispricing and slow diffusion of default-risk news is strongest. Industry ranking removes mechanical capital-structure differences across sectors.

considered.name: DownsideCashDebtCoverage
considered.expression: RATIO(TS_MIN(oancf, 5), lt)
considered.hypothesis: What matters for distress is not average cash generation but the worst cash flow a firm produced over a full cycle relative to its total obligations; high worst-case coverage marks quality-backed solvency and predicts higher returns, while firms whose trough operating cash flow cannot service liabilities underperform.
considered.reasoning: This builds the quality dimension (persistence of cash generation, measured as the 5-year minimum) directly into the distress denominator (total liabilities), so the signal is not decomposable into a cash-flow-margin effect or a leverage effect alone. Trough-based coverage is a forward-looking default proxy that accounting levels and averages miss, and investors appear to underweight downside cash-flow states.

considered.name: AccrualQualityXDebtBurden
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at)), IND_RANK(RATIO(ADD(dltt, dlc), at)))
considered.hypothesis: Earnings that are not backed by cash (high accruals) are especially informative about future trouble when the firm carries a heavy debt load, because accrual-inflated profits temporarily mask an inability to service obligations; the joint group of high-accrual, high-debt firms delivers low subsequent returns.
considered.reasoning: Accrual quality and debt burden are individually modest predictors, but their product identifies firms whose reported solvency is accounting-driven rather than cash-driven, which is where covenant violations and equity dilution cluster. Industry ranks control for sector-level working-capital and financing norms.

considered.name: DistressGatedCashSolvency
considered.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(NEG(re), 0), IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(MA(oancf, 3), lt)))
considered.hypothesis: Among firms with accumulated deficits (negative retained earnings, a classic distress marker), cross-sectional differences in smoothed operating cash flow relative to liabilities separate survivors from likely restructurers; the surviving cash generators earn a large positive spread over cash-poor distressed peers, while the same coverage differences matter little for firms with healthy retained earnings.
considered.reasoning: The indicator gate makes the signal an explicitly state-dependent interaction: non-distressed firms take the neutral value zero and only the distressed subsample is spread by cash-flow quality. Three-year averaging of oancf suppresses transitory cash swings so the ranking reflects durable solvency rather than one-off receipts.

considered.name: QualityLeverageAlignment
considered.expression: MUL(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(oancf, at)), IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(ADD(dltt, dlc), at)))
considered.hypothesis: The sign of the leverage-return relation flips with quality: for strong cash generators, debt is a compensated risk-and-discipline channel that predicts higher returns, whereas for weak cash generators the same debt is unpriced default risk that predicts lower returns. Aligned pairs (high cash flow with high debt, low cash flow with low debt) outperform misaligned pairs (low cash flow with high debt).
considered.reasoning: The product of two signed within-industry z-scores is positive exactly when capital structure is matched to cash-generating capacity, producing a pure interaction with (approximately) zero loading on either theme in isolation. This directly tests the sign-flip mechanism that a linear combination of quality and distress cannot express.

considered.name: NetDebtXCashMarginDecay
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(lt, che), at)), IND_RANK(NEG(TREND(RATIO(oancf, sale), 5))))
considered.hypothesis: Distress risk becomes acute when high net indebtedness is combined with a multi-year deterioration in cash conversion; the deteriorating trend signals that internal funds will not grow into the obligations, and such firms subsequently underperform, while high net debt paired with an improving cash margin is benign.
considered.reasoning: Cash net of the liquidity buffer (lt minus che) is the economically relevant distress stock, and the 5-year trend in operating cash flow to sales is the quality flow that determines whether that stock is sustainable. The interaction targets dynamic deterioration rather than a static level, a state that markets price with a lag.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: LossGatedGrossProfitCoverage
considered.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(NEG(pi), 0), IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), lt)))
considered.hypothesis: Among firms currently reporting a pretax loss (the distress state), the ones whose gross profit still covers a large fraction of total liabilities have a viable operating core and recover, while loss-makers whose gross profit is small relative to obligations face restructuring; for profitable firms this coverage difference carries little default information.
considered.reasoning: The pretax-loss indicator switches the signal on only in the distressed state and leaves healthy firms at the neutral value zero, so the predictive content is genuinely state-dependent rather than an unconditional gross-profitability effect. Gross profit (revt minus cogs) is the most persistent quality flow available and is unpolluted by the write-offs and one-off charges that drive reported losses.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: MarginDecayXCashDrain
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(TREND(RATIO(cogs, revt), 5)), IND_RANK(NEG(DELTA(RATIO(che, at), 1))))
considered.hypothesis: Distress is a process, not a level: firms whose cost-of-sales ratio has been trending up for years (eroding gross margin quality) and which are simultaneously drawing down their cash buffer are on a depletion path that the market prices with a lag, producing low subsequent returns.
considered.reasoning: Neither a slow margin slide nor a single year of cash decline is alarming alone; jointly they indicate that internal funds are shrinking exactly as unit economics deteriorate. Using a 5-year trend for the quality channel and a one-year change for the liquidity channel matches the different speeds at which operating deterioration and financing stress manifest.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: MarginStabilityXPretaxDebtCoverage
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(pi, lt)), IND_RANK(NEG(VOL(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), revt), 5))))
considered.hypothesis: Pretax earnings coverage of total liabilities is a much more reliable solvency measure when the underlying gross margin is stable; firms with strong coverage and stable margins are safe and richly rewarded, while weak coverage combined with volatile margins marks unpriced default risk.
considered.reasoning: Gross-margin volatility is the quality dimension that determines how much information a single year's coverage ratio contains, so multiplying the two ranks sharpens the distress ordering instead of restating it. Pretax income (pi) is used rather than net income to avoid tax and special-item noise in the coverage channel.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: NegativeWorkingCapitalProfitSort
considered.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(NEG(wcap), 0), IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at)))
considered.hypothesis: Negative working capital is ambiguous: for profitable firms it reflects efficient supplier financing and fast inventory turns, but for weakly profitable firms it is a liquidity shortfall. Sorting the negative-working-capital subsample on gross profitability should therefore generate a large spread, with efficient operators outperforming genuinely illiquid firms.
considered.reasoning: This tests a sign-interpretation flip rather than a monotone composite: the same balance-sheet configuration means opposite things depending on operating quality, which no single-theme signal can express. Firms with positive working capital are held at neutral zero so the spread is driven entirely by the conditioned subsample.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: CapitalConsumptionAdjustedLiquidity
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(oancf, dp), at)), IND_RANK(RATIO(che, lt)))
considered.hypothesis: Operating cash flow flatters firms whose cash flow is mostly the depreciation add-back; subtracting dp isolates cash earnings net of capital consumption, and this true cash-generating capacity is what makes a given cash-to-liabilities buffer sustainable rather than a one-time stock.
considered.reasoning: The interaction separates firms whose liquidity is replenished by real economic earnings from those holding a static cash stock while consuming their asset base, a distinction invisible to either cash-flow or liquidity signals alone. Depreciation intensity also proxies for the reinvestment obligation that competes with debt service.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: ChronicLossShortRunway
considered.expression: MUL(TS_SUM(INDICATOR(NEG(pi), 0), 5), IND_ZSCORE(NEG(RATIO(che, cogs))))
considered.hypothesis: Repeated pretax losses only become terminal when the cash balance is small relative to the firm's operating cost base; the number of loss years over five years times the shortness of the cash runway (che scaled by cogs) identifies firms most likely to dilute or default, which underperform.
considered.reasoning: Cash divided by cost of goods sold is an explicit runway concept that fuses the liquidity stock with the operating burn rate, and multiplying it by loss persistence rather than a single-year loss flag removes transitory-loss firms from the short leg. Firms with no loss years receive zero and stay neutral, so the spread comes from the chronically unprofitable tail.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: LiquidCoverageOfCurrentObligations
considered.expression: RATIO(ADD(che, SUB(oancf, dp)), lct)
considered.hypothesis: Near-term default risk is governed by the sum of the liquid stock (cash) and the sustainable cash flow net of capital consumption, measured against the obligations actually coming due (current liabilities); firms with high combined coverage earn higher returns than firms whose current liabilities exceed both their cash and their true cash earnings.
considered.reasoning: This fuses the quality flow (oancf net of the dp add-back) and the distress stock into a single economically interpretable coverage ratio rather than a product of ranks, which should raise coverage and stability relative to the gen-1 winner while preserving the mechanism. Current liabilities are strictly positive, so the ratio is well behaved and does not need the two-way ranking machinery.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: NetLiquidPositionXCashEarnings
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(oancf, dp), lt)), IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(che, dlc), at)))
considered.hypothesis: Refinancing risk, not total leverage, is the binding distress channel: firms whose cash exceeds short-term debt are immune to rollover shocks, and this immunity is most valuable when accompanied by cash earnings that actually service total liabilities. The joint group earns higher returns; net-short-cash firms with weak cash earnings underperform.
considered.reasoning: Replacing the cash-to-total-liabilities stock with the *net* liquid position (che minus dlc) changes the economic content from a liquidity buffer to rollover capacity, a distinct distress mechanism from the gen-1 winner. Scaling cash earnings by total liabilities rather than assets keeps both legs on a solvency footing.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: LossGatedCashRunway
considered.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(NEG(pi), 0), IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(che, cogs)))
considered.hypothesis: Among firms reporting a pretax loss, survival and returns are determined by how many periods of operating costs the cash balance can fund, not by the level of gross profitability; loss-makers with long runways are mispriced as if they were doomed and subsequently outperform loss-makers facing imminent financing needs.
considered.reasoning: This directly repairs the gen-1 loss-gate failure by keeping the state gate that isolated the distressed subsample but replacing the sorting variable with the liquidity-versus-burn concept that ChronicLossShortRunway's negative alpha already supported. Cash scaled by cost of goods sold is a runway measure that combines the distress stock with the operating cost base.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: ThinMarginCushionNoCash
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(cogs, revt)), IND_RANK(NEG(RATIO(che, lt))))
considered.hypothesis: A high cost-of-sales ratio means there is little gross-margin cushion to absorb a demand or input-price shock; when such a firm also holds almost no cash against its liabilities it has neither an operating nor a financial buffer, and its equity earns low subsequent returns.
considered.reasoning: This replaces the failed dynamic margin-decay design with the static level of the margin cushion, on the diagnosis that five-year trends and one-year cash changes were too noisy to identify the fragile group. The interaction is genuine: thin margins are tolerable with a cash buffer, and low cash is tolerable with fat margins, so only the joint state should predict underperformance.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: SmoothedCashEarningsXLiquidity
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(MA(RATIO(SUB(oancf, dp), at), 3)), IND_RANK(RATIO(che, lt)))
considered.hypothesis: The quality leg of the cash-earnings/liquidity interaction should reflect durable earning power rather than a single year's cash flow; three-year averaged cash earnings net of capital consumption, combined with the cash buffer against liabilities, should sharpen the distress ordering and improve the spread's reliability.
considered.reasoning: This isolates one design choice relative to the gen-1 winner - smoothing the quality channel - so the evaluation tells us whether its alpha came from persistent earning power or from transitory cash flow. Averaging also stabilises portfolio composition, which should raise ls_talpha and Sharpe even if the point alpha is similar.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: WeakestLinkSolvency
considered.expression: MIN(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(oancf, dp), lt)), IND_RANK(RATIO(che, lct)))
considered.hypothesis: Solvency is a weakest-link property: a firm is safe only if both its cash-earnings coverage of total liabilities and its cash coverage of near-term obligations are adequate, and strength in one dimension does not substitute for weakness in the other. The minimum of the two ranks should therefore predict returns better than their product.
considered.reasoning: The product form rewards firms that are extreme on one leg, whereas default is triggered by the binding constraint, so the MIN operator matches the economics of financial distress more literally. Testing it against the multiplicative winner isolates the functional form while holding the two economic channels fixed.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: GrossProfitRolloverWeakestLink
considered.expression: MIN(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), lt)), IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(che, dlc), at)))
considered.hypothesis: The weakest-link solvency mechanism should not depend on the cash-flow statement: gross profit relative to total liabilities measures the same durable capacity to service obligations, and a firm is safe only if that capacity and its net liquid position (cash minus short-term debt) are both adequate.
considered.reasoning: This tests whether the archive's best mechanism is about economic solvency or about the specific oancf-minus-dp construction, while nearly doubling coverage because gross profit is available for firms and periods where cash-flow items are missing. If the alpha survives at higher coverage, the mechanism is robust rather than a sample artefact.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: CashEarningsRolloverWeakestLink
considered.expression: MIN(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(oancf, dp), lt)), IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(che, dlc), at)))
considered.hypothesis: Combining the two strongest legs found so far - cash earnings net of capital consumption against total liabilities, and the net liquid position against assets - under a binding-constraint aggregation should deliver the sharpest distress ordering, because default requires only one of solvency or liquidity to fail.
considered.reasoning: WeakestLinkSolvency and NetLiquidPositionXCashEarnings each produced ~5.5% alpha with t above 3.6 but used different liquidity legs (che/lct versus che-minus-dlc) and different aggregations; this consolidates the better leg with the better aggregation. It is a deliberate one-step consolidation rather than a new channel, and its incremental value over both parents is directly measurable.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: TripleConstraintSolvency
considered.expression: MIN(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(oancf, dp), lt)), MIN(IND_RANK(RATIO(che, lct)), IND_RANK(RATIO(re, at))))
considered.hypothesis: Financial distress has three distinct binding constraints: insufficient cash earnings to service liabilities, insufficient cash for near-term obligations, and an absence of accumulated retained earnings (no equity cushion built from past profitability). A firm must clear all three to be genuinely safe, and the minimum across them should predict returns more sharply than any pair.

considered.name: BroadTroughCoverageDualLiquidity
considered.expression: MIN(IND_RANK(TS_MIN(RATIO(ADD(pi, dp), lt), 5)), MIN(IND_RANK(RATIO(che, act)), IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(che, dlc), at))))
considered.hypothesis: The same three-condition safety characterisation should hold on the broad sample when trough coverage is reconstructed from pretax income plus depreciation, delivering most of the winner's spread at roughly 50% higher coverage.
considered.reasoning: The pi-plus-dp coverage leg has consistently produced the highest alpha t-statistics (up to 4.80) at 0.124-0.140 coverage but weaker Sharpe ratios, and the missing ingredient in those tests was combining both liquidity legs at once. This is the deployable, wide-sample counterpart to signal 1 and tells us the cost of the cash-flow-statement requirement.

considered.name: CoverageStabilityCashComposition
considered.expression: MIN(IND_RANK(NEG(VOL(RATIO(SUB(oancf, dp), lt), 5))), IND_RANK(RATIO(che, act)))
considered.hypothesis: What protects a levered firm may be the low variability of its coverage rather than the level of its worst outcome: firms whose cash-earnings coverage barely moves have predictable debt service, and paired with liquid assets they should be the safest group.
considered.reasoning: Trough and volatility are different downside concepts - one is a worst realisation, the other a dispersion - and only the trough has been tested on the coverage series, while an early volatility test used gross margins rather than coverage. This distinguishes whether the market prices the depth of the worst outcome or the predictability of the series.
